post_understanding.summary: After routine Windows Updates and reboots on a SQL Server 2008 R2 SP3 machine, backups and queries became ~4–6x slower. Backup throughput dropped from ~192 MB/s to ~32 MB/s for a ~3 TB database on RAID10. Backup-to-NUL testing indicated the bottleneck was read speed. Ultimately, increasing MAXDOP from 4 to 8/16 restored both backup and query performance.
symptoms: NUL backup also slow, indicating read-side bottleneck
suspected_root_causes: MAXDOP set too low, limiting backup/compression/read-side parallelism
configuration change taking effect after reboot
less likely: network/NIC driver (ruled out by NUL backup)
less likely: storage/RAID controller behavior change
key_evidence: Backups to NUL showed the bottleneck seems to be the read speed
Changing MAXDOP from 4 to 8 (and 16) restored backup and query performance
Balanced vs High Performance power plan change did not affect backup speed
Throughput reduction scale (~6x) consistent across backups and queries
assumptions: ASSUMPTION: Backups use WITH COMPRESSION, increasing CPU involvement and potential sensitivity to parallelism.
ASSUMPTION: Backups are to local or fast destination; for isolation we will use backup to DISK and to NUL to separate read vs write.
ASSUMPTION: Original slowdown occurred without other heavy workloads; we will limit background noise to isolate effects.
ASSUMPTION: Database files are spread across multiple underlying disks (or multiple data files) to allow parallel read throughput in the baseline.
ASSUMPTION: SQL Server 2008 R2 SP3 on Windows Server (version not critical for reproduction), physical or VM with multiple logical CPUs (≥8).
ASSUMPTION: We will scale the database size down (e.g., 200–500 GB) for practicality; relative throughput changes are the validation target.
ASSUMPTION: MAXDOP change influences backup/compression/read-ahead behavior sufficiently to produce measurable throughput differences on SQL Server 2008 R2.

target_tables.purpose: Large heap/clustered table to provide substantial sequential read workload during backup and NUL backup.

columns.name: Filler
columns.role: bulk character data to increase row length

generated_data_plan.row_count: approx. 300 million rows (to achieve ~300–500 GB database size depending on payload fill)
generated_data_plan.distribution: uniform for DimA/DimB; EventDate spanning 12 months; Payload/Filler randomly filled to simulate realistic compression ratio
generated_data_plan.rationale: Create a sufficiently large dataset to engage sequential read throughput and backup compression behavior, enabling meaningful MB/s measurements and parallel read potential.

background_workloads.name: LightReadWriteNoise
background_workloads.inferred_from_post: OP focused on backups; to isolate, we assume minimal background load. However, small concurrent activity simulates typical production.
transactions_or_queries: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE TOP (1000) dbo.FactBig SET DimB = DimB + 1 WHERE DimA BETWEEN @a AND @b; COMMIT;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.FactBig WHERE EventDate BETWEEN @start AND @end;
SELECT SUM(CAST(SUBSTRING(Filler,1,10) AS INT)) FROM dbo.FactBig WITH (NOLOCK) WHERE DimA=@x;

anomaly_injection.name: LimitParallelism_MAXDOP1
anomaly_injection.method: Set MAXDOP to a low value to constrain parallelism that can impact backup/compression/read-side throughput on SQL Server 2008 R2.

parameters.precheck: Capture current MAXDOP via sys.configurations; record CPU count and NUMA layout.
parameters.set_maxdop: EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'max degree of parallelism', 1; RECONFIGURE;
parameters.backup_command_to_NUL: BACKUP DATABASE DBMAGS_PerfIO TO DISK = 'NUL' WITH COMPRESSION, STATS=5;
parameters.backup_command_to_DISK: BACKUP DATABASE DBMAGS_PerfIO TO DISK = 'C:\SQLBackups\DBMAGS_PerfIO_FULL.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, STATS=5;
metrics_to_collect: Backup throughput (MB/sec) from msdb.dbo.backupset and errorlog output
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats latencies and bytes read during backup
PerfMon: SQLServer:Backup Device Throughput/sec, PhysicalDisk Read/sec, Avg. Disk sec/Read
wait stats during backup (e.g., BACKUPIO, ASYNC_IO_COMPLETION, SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD)

safety_notes: Do not run on production. Changing MAXDOP affects all queries.
Revert MAXDOP to previous value after test.
Ensure sufficient disk space for on-disk backup runs; prefer NUL for read-isolation.
Limit test database size to available resources.

anomaly_injection.name: Optional_DisableReadAhead_TF652
anomaly_injection.method: Use undocumented trace flag 652 to disable read-ahead for the database to amplify read throttling (optional, only if MAXDOP alone does not yield a ~4x slowdown).

parameters.scope: Validate on isolated instance only; measure backup to NUL throughput before/after.

safety_notes: Trace flags affect engine behavior; only on non-production.

metrics.expected_change: decrease by 3–6x when MAXDOP=1 vs baseline (MAXDOP=8–16)
decrease by similar factor (assuming destination not bottlenecked)
lower overall CPU usage with MAXDOP=1 due to limited compression/read parallelism; higher with MAXDOP increased
may increase under constrained read parallelism; total Read/sec decreases markedly
increased waits indicating slower read progress when MAXDOP=1

query_or_transaction_effects: With MAXDOP=1, long-running analytical queries will also slow due to forced serial plans, reflecting post symptoms.
After restoring MAXDOP to 8–16, both backup and query performance return to baseline throughput levels.
validation_criteria: Under low MAXDOP, backup to NUL throughput drops by approximately the same factor as described (~4–6x) compared to higher MAXDOP.
Reverting MAXDOP to higher value restores throughput close to baseline.
Network destination does not influence NUL backup, confirming read-side bottleneck reproduction.
Observed behavior aligns with msdb backup history and PerfMon/DMV measurements collected during tests.

open_questions: Were backups performed WITH COMPRESSION at the time of slowdown and at baseline? If so, what was the compression ratio?
How many CPU cores/logical processors and NUMA nodes does the server have? What was the original MAXDOP value when backups slowed?
Were backups written to local disk, SAN, or network share? How many backup stripes were used?
How are database files laid out (number of data files, filegroups, LUNs)? Are they spread across multiple disks/LUNs?
Was max worker threads set to a non-default value? Any other instance-level settings changed around the reboot?
Is the server physical or virtual? Any concurrent host-level resource contention after the reboot?
What RAID controller, driver/firmware versions, and cache settings are in place? Any changes coinciding with Windows updates?
Did power plan or CPU frequency scaling change post-reboot despite attempting High Performance?
Were any trace flags enabled before/after the updates that could affect read-ahead or backup behavior?
